**Given:** The map $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ on the square $[0,1]^2$.

[F1] [[def-duffy-reference-triangle-map]]: $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ and $T=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le1\}$.

[F2] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: a map on an open Euclidean set is $C^1$ when all components are differentiable with continuous derivative entries; a local inverse is the inverse of a bijective restriction.

[F3] [[def-jacobian-determinant-of-a-c-one-map]]: the Jacobian determinant is the determinant of the derivative matrix.



1.1 For an increment $(h,k)$, $D(r+h,s+k)-D(r,s)=(h,sh+rk+hk)$. The linear part $(h,sh+rk)$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\s&r\end{pmatrix}$, while the remainder has Euclidean norm $|hk|\le(h^2+k^2)/2$; divided by $\|(h,k)\|_2=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ it tends to zero. Thus this is the total derivative. Its entries are continuous, so the polynomial extension is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ by [F2]; its determinant is $r$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $0\le r,s\le1$, then $0\le rs\le r\le1$, so $D(r,s)\in T$. Conversely, for $(x,y)\in T$ with $x>0$, $r=x$ and $s=y/x$ lie in $[0,1]$ and map to $(x,y)$; when $x=0$, $y=0$ and every $(0,s)$ maps to the vertex. For $r>0$, the displayed inverse is unique. This proves the image, inverse, and collapsed-edge claims. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice and a real exponent $\gamma>-1$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is the assumption used by the construction of Lebesgue measure.

[F1] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]: under [A1], Lebesgue measure is a measure and gives each interval its length.

[F2] [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]: products of measurable functions and indicators of Borel sets are measurable.

[F3] [[lem-real-power-improper-integral]]: for every $\gamma>-1$, $\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_\varepsilon^1x^\gamma\,dx=1/(\gamma+1)$.

[F4] [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]: $x^\gamma$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ and has derivative $\gamma x^{\gamma-1}$ there.

[F5] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: on a compact interval bounded away from zero, the integral of the derivative of a primitive equals its endpoint increment.

[F6] [[thm-riemann-criterion]]: a bounded function is Riemann integrable if Darboux upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close.

[F7] [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]: a bounded Riemann-integrable function is Lebesgue measurable and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: nonnegative measurable functions increasing pointwise to $g$ have integrals increasing to $\int g\,d\lambda$.



1.1 For each integer $n\ge1$, define $g_n(x)=x^\gamma$ on $[1/n,1]$ and $g_n(x)=0$ on $[0,1/n)$. By [F2] and [F4], $g_n$ is measurable and nonnegative. It is bounded and continuous on each side of its only possible jump at $1/n$; isolating that point in an interval of arbitrarily small length and using uniform continuity on the two remaining compact pieces makes its Darboux gap arbitrarily small, so [F6] gives Riemann integrability. [given, A1, F2, F4, F6, construct]

2.1 The equality of Riemann and Lebesgue integrals in [F7], followed by [F4] and [F5] on $[1/n,1]$, gives $\int g_n\,d\lambda=\int_{1/n}^1x^\gamma\,dx=(1-n^{-(\gamma+1)})/(\gamma+1)$. The sequence $g_n$ is nondecreasing and converges pointwise to $g_\gamma$. [F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply monotone convergence [F8] to step 2.1. Its limit is $1/(\gamma+1)$ by [F3], so $g_\gamma$ is integrable and the displayed value follows. The only choice assumption used is [A1], which supplies the underlying Lebesgue measure in [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, F8, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** One of the finite-interval, positive-half-line, or whole-line modes and its transformed integrand $\Phi$ from [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]], with $\Phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$.

[F1] [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]]: $\sinh t=(e^t-e^{-t})/2$, $\cosh t=(e^t+e^{-t})/2$, and the three maps and derivatives are displayed in its Definition.

[F2] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]: $e^t\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ and $e^t\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$.

[F3] [[thm-substitution]]: for a differentiable map on a compact interval and a continuous integrand on its image, the oriented definite integral changes variables with the derivative factor.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: compositions and the displayed sums, products, quotients with nonzero denominator, and reciprocals differentiate by the usual rules.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a differentiable real function with positive derivative on an interval is strictly increasing.



1.1 Differentiating $s(t)$ and $c(t)$ from their exponential formulas gives $s'(t)=c(t)>0$. Differentiating $\tanh u=(e^{2u}-1)/(e^{2u}+1)$ gives $\tanh'(u)=1/\cosh^2u>0$. The chain rule therefore gives the three positive derivatives in [F1]; [F5] makes each map strictly increasing. [F1, F4, F5, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 By [F2], $s(t)\to\pm\infty$ as $t\to\pm\infty$. Thus $\tanh((\pi/2)s(t))\to\pm1$, $\exp((\pi/2)s(t))$ tends to $0$ and $+\infty$ at the two ends, and $\sinh((\pi/2)s(t))\to\pm\infty$. Continuity, strict increase, and these endpoint limits prove the stated ranges and bijectivity. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $T>0$. On $[-T,T]$ each map is continuously differentiable and the relevant $f$ is continuous on its compact image, so [F3] gives $\int_{x(-T)}^{x(T)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{-T}^{T}\Phi(t)\,dt$. Applying the same identity to $|f|$ shows that the truncated absolute integrals equal $\int_{-T}^{T}|\Phi(t)|\,dt$. Since the maps are increasing, their endpoints tend to the target endpoints by step 2.1. Absolute integrability of $\Phi$ makes both limits converge, proving absolute convergence and the asserted identity. [F1, F3, given, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice and real parameters $\alpha,\beta>-1$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: the Countable Choice axiom is assumed.

[F1] [[lem-real-power-lebesgue-integrability]]: for every $q>-1$, $x\mapsto x^q$ on $(0,1]$, extended by zero at zero, is nonnegative and Lebesgue integrable with integral $1/(q+1)$.

[F2] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] and [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]: under [A1], Borel sets in $[-1,1]$ lie in the Lebesgue sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure is a measure there; an interval has measure its length ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F3] [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]: products, restrictions, and finite piecewise definitions on measurable sets preserve measurability.

[F4] [[def-measure-with-density]]: a nonnegative measurable density $w$ defines the measure $w\,d\lambda$ by $E\mapsto\int_Ew\,d\lambda$.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval attains its finite minimum and maximum.

[F6] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and positively homogeneous.



1.1 The density is nonnegative and Borel measurable by [F3], since it is continuous on $(-1,1)$ and differs from that continuous expression only at the two Borel endpoints. Put $M_\alpha=\max(1,2^\alpha)$ and $M_\beta=\max(1,2^\beta)$. On $[-1,0]$, $(1-t)^\alpha\le M_\alpha$, so the substitution $u=1+t$ and [F1] give $\int_{-1}^0w_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\lambda\le M_\alpha/(\beta+1)$. On $[0,1]$, $(1+t)^\beta\le M_\beta$, and $u=1-t$ gives $\int_0^1w_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\lambda\le M_\beta/(\alpha+1)$. Thus the total density integral is finite. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a positive Borel measure, and step 1.1 makes its total mass finite. If $U\subseteq[-1,1]$ is nonempty and relatively open, choose a nondegenerate closed interval $[c,d]\subset U\cap(-1,1)$. The density is continuous and strictly positive on $[c,d]$, so [F5] gives a minimum $m>0$ there. By [F2] and monotonicity [F6], $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}(U)\ge\int_{[c,d]}w_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\lambda\ge m(d-c)>0$. Therefore every point is in the relative support. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 For every $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $|t|^k\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, so [F6] gives $\int|t|^k\,d\mu_{\alpha,\beta}\le\mu_{\alpha,\beta}([-1,1])<\infty$ by step 1.1. This proves all moment claims. [F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

[F1] [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]]: the output is $h\sum_{k=-N_-}^{N_+}\Phi(kh)$.

**Given:** A real exponent $\alpha<2$, a continuous amplitude $q$ on the reference triangle $T$, and the map $D$ of [[def-duffy-reference-triangle-map]].

[F1] [[def-duffy-reference-triangle-map]] and [[lem-duffy-reference-map-jacobian-and-image]]: $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ maps the square to $T$, is one-to-one with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y/x)$ for $r>0$, and has determinant $r$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|(r,rs)\|_2=r\sqrt{1+s^2}$ for $r>0$.

[F3] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-compact-jordan-sets]]: on a compact truncated region where the map is one-to-one with nonzero Jacobian, the integral changes by the absolute Jacobian determinant.

[F4] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] and [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]: the continuous function $G$ is bounded on the compact square, and $u\mapsto u^{-\alpha/2}$ is continuous for $u>0$.

[F5] [[lem-real-power-improper-integral]]: if $\gamma>-1$, then $\int_0^\varepsilon r^\gamma dr=\varepsilon^{\gamma+1}/(\gamma+1)$.

[F6] [[thm-real-power-laws]]: positive-base powers satisfy $(ab)^u=a^ub^u$ and $(a^v)^u=a^{vu}$.

[F7] [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]: the composition and product of the continuous functions in $G$ remain continuous.

Thus its restriction to the compact Jordan rectangle $[\varepsilon,1]\times[0,1]$ satisfies [F3]; on its image $\|(x,y)\|_2\ge\varepsilon$, so the integrand is continuous and bounded there. 2.1 The function $G$ is continuous on $[0,1]^2$ by [F4] and [F7], so let $M=\max|G|<\infty$. Hence the truncated integrals have an absolutely convergent limit and the displayed identity follows from step 1.1. [F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The same bound applies to any neighborhood of the vertex contained in $0\le x<\varepsilon$, and every sufficiently small Euclidean ball about $(0,0)$ is contained in such a set. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, $a<b$, $n\ge1$, $\alpha,\beta>-1$, nonnegative integers $m_a,m_b$, $h\in C^{2n}([a,b])$, and positive integers $q_a,q_b$ with $q_a(\alpha+1)-1>2n$ and $q_b(\beta+1)-1>2n$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: this axiom is used only to form the Lebesgue-density Gaussian rule.
